newsitem.title: USA: Wall St bull market roars ahead as rate fears fade.
newsitem.headline: Wall St bull market roars ahead as rate fears fade.

text.p: Wall Street's bull market got a jump-start Friday as fresh economic data pointed to moderating economic growth and tame inflation, raising hopes the Fed will not raise interest rates later this month.

"Goldilocks is back -- the economy is not too hot or too cold. Looking at the T-bill curve, the market consensus is there will be no tightening. Stocks are going straight up today. This is the kind of environment where we'll have a Dow 6000 by the election," said David Shulman, chief equity strategist at Salomon Brothers.
The Dow industrials jumped 34 points or 0.59 percent to 5805 within minutes after the opening bell, topping 5800 for the first time in history.
The long bond rose 1-11/32, knocking its yield down to 6.96 percent -- below the psychologically key seven percent level.

Bonds and stocks roared ahead after the consumer price index, closely watched by the Fed and Wall Street, rose 0.1 percent for August, below the expected 0.2 percent. August retail sales rose 0.2 percent, well below the anticipated 0.7 percent.

"Today's numbers look as if the economy is slowing to a more moderate, more sustainable pace. Even though there's some pressure on the wholesale level and wages, it's not showing at the all-important consumer level," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.
"So, if you're looking at the financial markets, there's no better combination. The decision is not whether to be in stocks, the question is which ones, or bonds."
Johnson added, "yesterday, I strongly suspected the Fed would raise rates by a quarter point. Today, I'm not so sure."

As for which stocks, Johnson said, "There's something for everyone. If there's one theme, it's we're headed to a 1997 where the growth rate of profits will be down significantly from after-tax corporate profits of up nine percent for 1996 to up three percent in 1997. Look for those companies whose earnings would be higher in 1997 and where earnings estimates are being raised, not reduced."
"You buy Intel, not Motorola. You buy DuPont and International Paper and Caterpillar , not Alcoa," he said.
But others remain wary of the near-term outlook for stocks.

"On a short-term basis, technicals are driving the market. Bonds are up but long term, rates are still near seven percent and we'll be getting more (corporate earnings) preannouncements which would be a negative. The market is shrugging that off," said Ricky Harrington, a technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane.
"Mutual fund cash (into stocks) rose sharply last month so demand for the time being continues to be positive."
Harrington added, "I wouldn't be surprised to see some profit-taking and we have triple witching next week. We're getting portfolio switching now."
Michael Metz, Oppenheimer and Co's chief investment strategist, remains cautious. "We had a bang up opening but how sustainable is another matter. We could have new highs and keep them."

He sees the market "in a trading range, extending the upper limits. In the background, we still have the problem of having an economy that is stronger than the Fed desires. We have strong energy and food prices, upward pressure on wages, and downward pressure on margins."
Stocks and bonds subsequently extended their gains in heavy mid-morning action.
